claims.text: Integrated in situ high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction with fast detectors and complementary measurements can simultaneously monitor high-temperature oxidation kinetics and phase evolution in real time.
The materials examined are high-temperature alloys or ceramics initially in a single-phase solid-solution state.
An in situ high-energy synchrotron XRD setup can be operated during exposure to high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
In situ synchrotron XRD can be integrated with TGA or in situ spectroscopy during oxidation exposure.
Temperatures from approximately 750 °C to above 1200 °C are relevant to high-temperature phase stability and transformation studies.
Oxidation and phase transformations can occur dynamically under the stated high-temperature reactive conditions.
Diffraction peak shifts, intensity changes, and new peaks reflect oxide-layer formation and phase-transformation events.
Fast high-energy XRD can capture transient structural changes during high-temperature oxidation.
Thermogravimetric mass changes can quantify oxidation kinetics.
Simultaneous structural and kinetic measurements permit direct temporal correlation of oxidation onset and progression with phase stability or transformation events.
The integrated method will reveal synchronized evolution of oxide formation and phase transitions or phase-stability retention.
The integrated method provides a more complete picture than separate ex situ analyses.
Separate ex situ or non-integrated measurements can miss dynamic correlations between oxidation and phase evolution.
Detector time resolution can limit the effectiveness of the integrated method.
The spatial resolution of complementary techniques can limit the integrated method.
Instrument-integration challenges and restricted setup temperature ranges can constrain observations.
The sensitivity and time resolution required to detect very rapid oxidation or subtle phase shifts are not fully established.
Synchronization fidelity between XRD and complementary measurements is uncertain.
The method can be tested at 750 °C, 900 °C, and 1200 °C by continuously recording XRD patterns and mass changes.
Failure to observe a time-correlated association between TGA-measured oxidation and XRD-measured phase changes would reject the stated method-performance hypothesis.
